items.title: Woman’s Bold Biblical Mission to ‘Capture … Souls From Hell’
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "I want to see people come to Jesus."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Ministry leader Bunni Pounds is on a mission to encourage Americans to crack open their Bibles and learn more about the Lord.

Pounds, founder of the newly minted Bunni Pounds Ministries, told CBN News her previous mission of motivating Christians to vote has been replaced by efforts to spark interest in the Bible. Her America Reads the Bible initiative earlier this year ignited Bible interest among millions of people, with three million watching as 500 national leaders read through the entire Bible.

“I’ve spent the last seven years of my life trying to mobilize Christians to pray, vote, engage through Christians Engaged,” she said. “But America Reads the Bible shifted my entire life and our team, and we just realized there’s a root problem more below the surface than just Christians engaging and voting.”

Pounds believes America has a biblical literacy problem. And seeing how America Reads the Bible took form motivated her to seek more of a biblical impact.

“It impacted so many people in this country,” she said of the effort. “And I realized we’ve got to pour gasoline on this. We’ve got to really reach the younger generation, and so we launched the ministry with the idea that we are going to lead thousands of people through a Bible study created with Great American Pure Flix with this content.”

Pounds and her ministry are inviting people to go through the Bible together over a 24-week period starting Jan. 1; she’s calling the effort The Whole Bible Live. Pounds is also planning yet another national event in 2028, along with other local efforts.

“At the end of the day, I want to see people come to Jesus,” Pounds said, explaining what success for her new ministry might look like. “I want to see people be discipled, and I want to see people become disciple makers, and so success looks like hundreds of thousands of people, in the next five years, going through the Bible, becoming the leaders that God’s called them to be, understanding who they truly are in Christ, and taking on the culture, and bringing truth into culture.”

Pounds said young people are hungry and “desperate for God” — and she delivered an important reminder for believers.

“We’re not fighting against people that we disagree with,” she said. “God is after people’s hearts. He’s trying to capture their souls from hell.”

Pounds said she believes America is at a turning point and that Christians need to be encouraging everyone to turn to the Lord. She encouraged people to go to Bunni Pounds Ministries and take part in the Whole Bible Live.

“We need Jesus in this moment,” Pounds said.

items.title: Are Demons Real? New Data Reveals Americans’ Experience With Spiritual Attacks
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Spiritual warfare is a real part of the human experience, and the Bible explicitly details how events in the spiritual realm affect people.

“For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the powers of this dark world and against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms,” Ephesians 6:12 (NIV) reads, with verse 13 continuing: “Therefore put on the full armor of God, so that when the day of evil comes, you may be able to stand your ground, and after you have done everything, to stand.”

The question isn’t if people will experience spiritual warfare; it’s when. A new survey from the American Bible Society (ABS) explores what Americans believe about spiritual warfare, specifically measuring how many people believe they have faced such attacks (watch CBN’s documentary “Investigating the Supernatural: Angels and Demons” today).

Dr. John Plake, editor-in-chief of the State of the Bible series and chief innovation officer at ABS, told CBN News that around 1-in-4 Americans report facing spiritual warfare.

“We saw real difference here across levels of faith participation,” he said. “About a fourth — 26% — of American adults say they’ve had that experience.”

He continued, “[Fifty-eight percent] of practicing Christians would agree with that statement, casual Christians, 28%, nominal Christians, 24%, and then non-Christians, 10%.”

The topic itself is quite fascinating, as Plake said it’s sometimes hard to quantify what a spiritual attack denotes. And since there’s not “a lot of deep data” there’s not qualitative information to help understand what respondents believe a spiritual attack looked like or entailed.

“I’m sure these people do have stories that they can tell about times when they felt like the negative experiences that they were having couldn’t be attributed just to natural causes, that there was some form of spiritual opposition that was going on,” Plake said. “And to see that incidence be that high, I was pretty fascinated by it.”

Another factor ABS was able to screen for was people’s reaction to a perceived spiritual attack — and those statistics were equally interesting.

“So 74% of people who [said they faced attack] said that the way they respond to spiritual attack is that they pray,” Plake said. “I think that makes a lot of sense, right? When spiritual attacks come, you may not be in a particular context where it’s easy to do much else, but you can always pray.”

The second-highest percentage was 36%, who said they declare Christ’s authority.

“There is this kind of sense that … they’re aware they’re in a spiritual battle, that their opposition isn’t … the person who may be opposing them at the moment,” Plake said. “But actually, there’s a spiritual thing going on here, and so they declare Christ’s authority.”

Next came the 24% who said they listen to praise and worship music, but then there’s the smallest — and most concerning — percentage: the 15% who said that they meditate on or quote Scripture.

“I would have hoped that would be a little bit higher,” Plake said. “And I think it also presents an opportunity for pastors and church leaders to recognize, ‘Hey, there are a lot of people, particularly in the church, who are having these experiences, and how can we equip them biblically to respond when they’re facing these kinds of spiritual attacks or moments of opposition, or even when there’s a need for a miraculous healing?'”

For more on this topic, watch “Investigating the Supernatural: Angels and Demons.”

items.title: Joel Smallbone and the Brother He Drifted From Just Made a Movie About Brothers at War
items.author: Cameron Strang
items.summary: At one point, Joel Smallbone and his brother Ben went their separate ways. “You could argue we ended up on our own sort of opposite sides of life’s battlefield,” Smallbone says. What brought them back together was a movie about the same thing. “I remember saying, wouldn’t it be fascinating if two br
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

At one point, Joel Smallbone and his brother Ben went their separate ways. “You could argue we ended up on our own sort of opposite sides of life’s battlefield,” Smallbone says. What brought them back together was a movie about the same thing.

“I remember saying, wouldn’t it be fascinating if two brothers who’ve had ideological differences and creative differences came back together behind the camera to tell a story about two brothers that end up on opposite sides of a literal war?”

That movie is Drummer Boy, a Revolutionary War Christmas musical that opened in theaters Nov. 6. Joel and Ben co-directed it, and Joel plays Jeremiah Clem. The cast includes Ioan Gruffudd and Melora Hardin (Jan from The Office).

It took a while. Smallbone, who sings in for KING + COUNTRY with his brother Luke, pitched it to Lionsgate on March 10, 2020, and, by his account, the studio nearly greenlit it.

“And then March the 13th happened and the world shut down,” he says. Unsung Hero came first and the musical waited. Someone eventually reminded him 2026 is America’s 250th birthday. “Well, maybe it was just always meant to be now.”

The Movie That Wrote Him

“Do you write the movie or does the movie write you?” Smallbone asks. “There’s never been a movie that’s written me more than Drummer Boy.”

He lists the evidence. “We came up with this rendition of ‘The Little Drummer Boy’ at the beginning of our career. We’re called for KING + COUNTRY, which is a British mantra. We wore these revolutionary-type uniforms for many years. I’m in a band with my brother. This is a movie about brothers on opposite sides of the battlefield. I’m a musician. It’s a musical. You just see all of these breadcrumbs.”

When he got stuck on the lead character, a director asked him who he was. “I’ve got a rescuer complex,” he says. “A bit of a savior complex. And so I just wrote all of it into the film.”

Unsung Hero was literally about his family, so it’s fair to ask why this one feels more like him. His answer is allegory.

“Jesus was the allegory guy,” Smallbone says. “He made up stories for a living, you know? I see myself more in it because it’s all allegorical about our life, and America, and me being an immigrant and in a mixed marriage, and brothers on other sides of the battlefield.”

A Musical for People Who Hate Musicals

“I need to clear up something to the musical haters,” he says. About 30 minutes of the film are musical moments, “very personal expressions of heartache or love or loss.” He calls it “Hamilton meets The Patriot meets Pride and Prejudice.”

His rule for when a character should sing is simple. “The best musicals put language to things that you couldn’t express through dialogue. The worst musicals just sing the whole time. And I’m like, just stop. That’s not life.”

His example is Chris Martin writing “Fix You” after Gwyneth Paltrow’s father died. “You have to express yourself in grief, in pain, and a lot of times it comes through music.”

The same logic runs through the film. One character, an enslaved woman, sings her way through being stuck. “She’s stuck and she’s enslaved and she needs to sing about it to understand it better,” he says.

Two Brothers Behind the Camera

The shoot gave the co-directing brothers plenty of challenges to overcome. The last day of filming was the big argument between Jeremiah and Emmaline on a hillside, in 40 mph winds.

“She’s in this dress, almost getting blown off the hillside,” Smallbone says. “We were like, I don’t know if we’re gonna use any of this.” The wind made the cut. “The tragedy of the bad weather actually created a third layer to the scene.”

The argument matters to the story. Jeremiah, Smallbone says, is “not practicing what he’s preached.” His father taught him “no boy or girl or slave or free, because all in one in Christ are we,” an echo of Galatians 3:28. Jeremiah is “chasing, basically, imperialism and hierarchy and climbing the ladder by who he’s gonna marry.”

Heat was the opposite problem. On a day he puts at 87 degrees, the Irish cast and crew, who spend winter swimming in a rocky ocean, wilted. “You would have thought we were in New Mexico, or Las Vegas on a hot summer,” he says. “A couple of people were hospitalized.”

Drummer Boy had company on the Irish shoot. Smallbone played a villain in a small role in Young Washington, a film about the young George Washington made there, and he’s at peace with the overlap. He points to something Rick Rubin says: “Don’t be upset if that idea that you thought of comes to life through someone else’s vision. It’s not that they stole your idea, it’s that the time had come for the idea.”

Young Washington paid off for him, too. He kept the red British uniform, he says, and “they let me run onto the sets outside of filming, and they let me borrow one of their featured extras” to shoot a sizzle reel that “ended up helping get Drummer Boy funded.” He wandered the island in character and apologized to anyone who gave him a look. “I’d go, ‘Hey, I’m really sorry. I’m Australian. I’m not even from England.’”

Forgiveness is the theme he says he’s proudest of in the film. “What does it mean to be forgiven by God? What does it mean to forgive yourself? What does it mean to forgive others?” Smallbone asks. “You can’t have freedom without forgiveness.”

It was personal for the Smallbones, too. He and Ben had to find their way back to each other before they could make a movie about it. “It was really Drummer Boy when it came back around,” he says, “and we started talking again.”

items.title: Evangelization Is Our Responsibility
items.author: Mark Bradford
items.summary:
Mark Bradford

We can either pass by those in need, or we can embrace our neighbor in friendship and with the ministry of love that Jesus has entrusted to all of us who bear his name.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Mark Bradford

Those who attend Mass during the week know that through the fall we have been feasting on the richness of Luke’s Gospel, which unfolds the remarkable pattern of Jesus’s messianic mission first proclaimed in the fourth chapter.

After his baptism and temptations in the desert, Jesus returns to his hometown in Nazareth where we find a crowd gathered to hear him. Luke tells us, 

He stood up to read, and the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was given to him. He unrolled the scroll and found the place where it was written:

“The Spirit of the Lord is upon me,
because he has anointed me
to bring good news to the poor.
He has sent me to proclaim release to the captives
and recovery of sight to the blind,
to let the oppressed go free,
to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor.”

When he finished, “The eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him, all eyes were fixed on him,” and he said to them, “Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:16–21). Their initial response to him was admiration, but that quickly turned to rage when he reminded them that God’s grace has never been confined to those who believed they were entitled to it. His examples of Elijah and Elisha ministering to Gentiles resulted in their trying to kill him. Belonging, it seems, is no guarantee that one will understand or welcome God’s salvific work. 

After Jesus escapes the mob, he returns to Capernaum and resumes his ministry, and in Luke’s Gospel, the miracles come rapidly, one after the other, as testimony that his claim in the synagogue in Nazareth was true. Soon, Jesus expands his circle by choosing twelve men as his apostles whom he entrusts with a share in his mission. Luke tells us that “Jesus called the twelve together and gave them power and authority over all demons and to cure diseases, and he sent them out to proclaim the kingdom of God and to heal” (Luke 9:1–2).

But sometime after the apostles returned from their first venture, there was some confusion among them. John approached Jesus with a complaint. He said, “Master, we saw someone casting out demons in your name, and we tried to stop him, because he does not follow with us.” Jesus’s response to him was, “Do not stop him; for whoever is not against you is for you” (Luke 9:49–50). In his hometown of Nazareth, Jesus himself was an insider rejected by his own people. Now we have Jesus affirming the work of this anonymous exorcist who acts in the name of Jesus, but the apostles regard him as outside their circle. 

That scene is rich. If the apostles were thinking that their ministry was exclusive, they learned a lesson in humility that day. Luke does not tell us how this man came to act in Jesus’s name. We can only guess that he was acting on his own initiative—not casting out demons by his own authority but by the power of Jesus’s name. What he does tell us is membership in the apostles’ inner circle was not the condition Jesus imposed for allowing his work to flourish—there is a place for others.

John’s complaint about this man came immediately after the apostles were arguing among themselves over which of them was the greatest. Jesus “was aware of their inner thoughts” and resolved the dispute by bringing a little child into their midst to teach them that the key to ministry is humility: “The least among all of you is the greatest” (Luke 9:48). 

After Jesus announces his messianic mission in chapter 4, he begins to expand his circle to share his ministry with others, including spiritual gifts that would give witness to their preaching. Jesus calls his apostles and commissions them to go out to preach and heal in his name. Later in chapter ten, he appoints seventy others and sends them out in pairs as additional “laborers into his harvest.” 

In our own time, the Second Vatican Council affirmed the vocation of the laity in their Decree on the Apostolate of the Laity, Apostolicam Actuositatem. They wrote that, “The laity derive the right and duty to the apostolate from their union with Christ the head,” and “they are assigned to the apostolate by the Lord Himself” (3). 
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

In one of his most revered parables, Jesus discusses with a Jewish lawyer what he must do to inherit eternal life. The lawyer provides the right response: to love the Lord with all your heart, soul, strength, and mind, and your neighbor as yourself. But Jesus responds to the lawyer’s question about who his neighbor is with a fantastic story of an injured man who had fallen into the hands of robbers and was left on the road beaten, robbed, and half dead. In the story, the religious figures—a priest and a Levite—both passed by him, making sure to cross to the other side of the road to avoid him. But a Samaritan, an outsider, stopped to care for this man. 

Jesus gives no indication of the injured man’s identity, and he only identifies the one who helped him as a Samaritan. As St. John says in his Gospel, “Jews do not share things in common with Samaritans” (John 4:9), but this Samaritan’s deep compassion becomes the central lesson in the story: Our neighbor is anyone in need, and when we see another person in need we must help—without distinction. The “insiders” failed in their obligation to the law, and the “outsider” provided a vivid reminder of what love really entails. 

The Roman Catholic Church has built an incredible network of support through its social services, and we Catholics can be tempted to assume that the charitable institutions of the Church will manage our charitable works for us. The anonymous exorcist makes clear that the Church’s institutional work does not replace our personal obligation to be evangelists.

There are many people near to us—even in our parishes—who still await an encounter with Jesus’s liberating mercy. The poor, unemployed, and homeless are waiting for relief from the burden of their poverty. Those who are captive to sin long for an encounter with the mercy of Christ, and the sick, disabled, and impaired search for welcome and friendship. The anonymous exorcist, the Good Samaritan, and Vatican II all show us that ministry isn’t the responsibility of a select few who hold positions within the institutional Church. Evangelization—bringing the good news of the messiah into the darkness of the current age—is all our responsibility.

Jesus presents us with an example of the demand of discipleship in the parable of the good Samaritan, and he leaves us with a choice. We can either pass by those in need, as the priest and Levite did, or we can embrace our neighbor in friendship and with the ministry of love that Jesus has entrusted to all of us who bear his name.

items.title: WOF 548 | The Meaning of Catholic Ordination
items.author: Dr. Matthew Petrusek
items.summary:
Dr. Matthew Petrusek

Why do Catholics uphold this difference between what we call clergy and laity, and where does it come from?
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Matthew Petrusek

Welcome back to the Word on Fire Show. I’m Matthew Petrusek, senior director of the Word on Fire Institute and the host of the Word on Fire Show. Thank you for joining us. One of the fundamental dividing lines within Christianity is marked by a disagreement about whether certain people (specifically men, within Catholicism) not only have a distinctive calling or vocation to serve the Church but are able to do so by means of ordination—that is, in a way that fundamentally or, to use philosophical language, ontologically distinguishes them from the flock they serve. Why do Catholics uphold this difference between what we call clergy and laity? Where does this distinction originate, and how can it respond to the critique that it is inegalitarian, elitist, and even sexist? Put more positively, what is it that bishops, priests, and deacons—the only ordained ministers within Catholicism—can contribute to the life of faith and the path toward salvation that no one else can? Here to explain the nature and meaning of ordination and the process by which it takes place, and to reflect on his recent experience ordaining new deacons into the Catholic Church at St. Peter’s Basilica in Rome, is Bishop Robert Barron.
